tracks.legalName: Petition for Expungement of Misdemeanor Records (Mont. Code Ann. tit. 46, ch. 18, pt. 11)

controllingAuthority.summary: Title 46, chapter 18, part 11 lets a person petition a district court to expunge the records of one or more misdemeanour convictions entered in Montana state courts, whether in one court or several and whether in one case or several (§ 46-18-1104(1)). The petition is once in a lifetime: a person who has already had records expunged under the part, or who has already petitioned, may not petition again (§ 46-18-1104(1) and (2)). Venue is a district court in a judicial district where at least one of the convictions occurred (§ 46-18-1105), so a participant with convictions in several districts chooses among them. Section 46-18-1106(1) requires notice to every prosecution office that prosecuted an offence for which expungement is requested, and § 46-18-1106(2) gives that office fourteen days from receiving the petition to attempt to notify any victim. Section 46-18-1107 creates a presumption in favour of expungement where the person is not detained, charged or subject to pending charges as verified by the prosecution office, and either five years have passed since completion of the sentencing terms with no conviction of any offence in Montana, another state or federal court, or the person meets the military condition in § 46-18-1107(1)(b). Section 46-18-1108(1) removes the presumption entirely for convictions for assault, partner or family member assault, stalking, sexual assault, violation of a protective order, DUI however named, or any offence carrying a statutorily enhanced penalty for driving under the influence, and § 46-18-1108(2) then directs the court to weigh age at the offence, elapsed time, rehabilitation, likelihood of reoffending and any other relevant factor. Section 46-18-1109(2) lets the presumption be overcome on a determination that the interests of public safety demand dismissal, and the standard throughout is a preponderance of the evidence. The court may expunge all, some or none of the offences (§ 46-18-1110(1)). Section 46-18-1103(1) defines expungement as permanently destroying, deleting or erasing a record from the DOJ criminal history record information system, and § 46-18-1110(2)(a) directs the arresting agency, the prosecutor's office and the clerk of the convicting court to permanently seal their own records. Crucially, § 46-18-1110(2)(b) puts the second stage on the participant: the person whose records are being expunged sends the order, fingerprints and the DOJ form to those agencies and to the Department of Justice. No amendment since Ch. 384, L. 2019; § 46-18-1101 is repealed.

exclusions: Felony convictions. Part 11 does not reach them and Montana has no general felony expungement route.
Convictions from out-of-state courts, federal courts or Tribal courts, which are outside Part 11.
Non-conviction records, which go to the non-conviction removal or automatic removal tracks.
Marijuana-related convictions, which the judiciary packet expressly excludes and which go to the two MMRTA tracks.
A person who has already had records expunged under this part, or who has already petitioned once (§ 46-18-1104(1) and (2)). This is a once-in-a-lifetime petition.
Fingerprint records and data maintained for investigative purposes, expressly outside the § 46-18-1103(2)(b) definition of a record.

Not an outright bar but a defeated presumption: § 46-18-1108(1) removes the presumption for assault under § 45-5-201, partner or family member assault under § 45-5-206, stalking under § 45-5-220, sexual assault under § 45-5-502, violation of a protective order under § 45-5-626, DUI however named under Title 61, ch. 8, pt. 10, or any offence carrying a statutorily enhanced penalty as a result of driving under the influence.

waitingPeriods.duration: Five years since the person completed the sentencing terms for the offences for which expungement is requested, including payment of any financial obligations and successful completion of court-ordered treatment, with no conviction of any offence in Montana, another state or a federal court during that period.

None. The five-year clock does not apply where the person has applied to a United States military academy, has applied to enlist in the armed forces or national guard, or is currently serving and is being held back from enlisting or from holding a position because of a prior conviction.

units.label: District-court petition for expungement of misdemeanor records
units.description: The court stage. A Petition for Expungement of Misdemeanor Records, a certificate of service and a proposed order, filed in a district court in a judicial district where at least one conviction occurred. Title 46, chapter 18, part 11 prescribes no form; § 46-18-1111 grants rulemaking authority but no statewide expungement form has been adopted under it, and the only published petition and order — ER-100 and ER-200 — are a Montana Legal Services Association and Access to Justice Commission work product licensed for non-commercial use only and are neither mandatory nor usable in a paid packet. LegalEase therefore drafts its own, which is both lawful and cleaner. The petition pleads the participant's identity and contact details; that at least one conviction occurred in the district, establishing venue; each conviction with crime, case number, conviction date and court; completion of all sentencing terms including financial obligations and court-ordered treatment; that the petitioner is not detained, charged or subject to pending charges; that the petitioner has not previously petitioned for or received expungement under the part; the years since the last conviction or the military basis; and that the petitioner will be fingerprinted to validate identity under § 46-18-1104(3). The prayer asks that the listed misdemeanours be expunged from the DOJ criminal history record information system, that the arresting agencies, prosecutors' offices and clerks permanently seal their records under § 46-18-1110(2)(a), and that the clerk seal the record of the expungement matter itself. The certificate of service covers every county attorney and city attorney office that prosecuted a case in the petition. The proposed order leaves the date and signature blank for the judge.

units.label: DOJ CRISS expungement submission after the court order
units.description: The Department of Justice stage, and a genuinely separate legal unit: a different destination, a different actor's form, and a participant submission the statute places on the participant rather than on the court or the clerk. Section 46-18-1110(2)(b) requires the person whose records are being expunged to send the order, fingerprints and a form prepared by the Department of Justice to the arresting agency, the prosecutor, the clerk of the convicting court and the Department. LegalEase completes the participant-owned fields of the CRISS Expungement/Removal Request Form with the misdemeanour expungement request type selected, and supplies the mailing checklist, the § 46-18-1110(2)(b) distribution list and the verification steps. The FD-258 blue applicant fingerprint card is a physical prerequisite of this stage — cards are free from DOJ CRISS but there is a fee to have prints taken — and it is sequenced at the FRONT of the participant's task list rather than surfaced at the end. It is required before the CRISS submission, never before LegalEase generates the court packet. Without this stage a signed court order leaves the conviction sitting on the participant's background check.

geography.venue: A Montana district court in a judicial district where at least one of the convictions occurred (§ 46-18-1105). The underlying convictions will usually have been entered in Justice, Municipal or City Court, but the expungement petition goes to District Court. Where convictions span several districts the participant chooses among them, and the choice has strategic consequences and is never auto-selected.

destination.name: Montana District Court, then the Department of Justice
destination.detail: Unit 1 is filed with the clerk of the chosen district court. Unit 2 is mailed to Montana Department of Justice, Division of Criminal Investigation, CRISS Expungement, 2225 11th Ave., P.O. Box 201403, Helena, MT 59620. Phone (406) 444-3625. Email dojcriss@mt.gov.

components.notes: Petition for Expungement of Misdemeanor Records, LegalEase-drafted. Caption with the petitioner's name, mailing address, phone and email; the court line for the chosen judicial district and county; 'In re Expungement of Misdemeanor Records of: ____, Petitioner'; case number left blank for the clerk. Cites Title 46, ch. 18, pt. 11 generally, § 46-18-1104(1) for the right to petition, § 46-18-1105 for venue, § 46-18-1107 for the presumption, § 46-18-1108 where it does not apply, and §§ 46-18-1103(1) and 46-18-1110 for the relief. Verified by declaration under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of Montana. ER-100 is not used and is not reproduced.

Certificate of service, LegalEase-drafted, reciting the § 46-18-1106(1) duty and identifying every prosecution office that prosecuted an offence in the petition, with mailing address and email, the date of service and the method. Montana files first and then serves the file-stamped petition; do not carry over another state's serve-then-file sequence. Victims are notified by the prosecution office under § 46-18-1106(2), never by the participant.

Proposed order, LegalEase-drafted, on the same caption. Findings of good cause under Title 46, ch. 18, pt. 11; ordered paragraphs granting expungement of the enumerated convictions, directing the Department of Justice to permanently destroy, delete or erase those records from the criminal history record information system, directing the law-enforcement agencies, prosecutors' offices and courts involved to permanently seal all records in their possession, recording that the petitioner is responsible for sending the order, fingerprints and the DOJ form under § 46-18-1110(2)(b), and directing the clerk to seal the record of the expungement case. Date and signature lines are left blank for the presiding judge. ER-200 is not used and is not reproduced.

Unit 2's CRISS Expungement/Removal Request Form, updated 29 April 2024 and retained by Master Library Edition 1.1 as the Montana supporting-process asset. LegalEase completes the participant-owned fields — full legal name, date of arrest or fingerprinting, the list of charges, date of birth, the optional last four digits of the Social Security number, return address, phone and email — and selects the misdemeanour expungement request type. The signature and date are left for the participant. This is a genuine agency form with no use restriction and is what § 46-18-1110(2)(b) means by a form prepared by the department of justice.

Sequenced participant instructions across both units. Front-loaded: obtain the DOJ CRISS criminal background check; run BOTH Montana Public Access Portal searches, District Courts and Courts of Limited Jurisdiction, because some misdemeanour convictions do not appear on the CRISS check; obtain the judgments from each convicting court; and obtain the free FD-258 blue applicant fingerprint card from DOJ CRISS and have prints taken, expecting a fee. Then the court stage: confirm local district court filing rules with the clerk, file, pay the fee or seek a waiver, serve every prosecuting office with the file-stamped petition. Then the DOJ stage: obtain certified copies of the order and judgment, complete and mail the CRISS form with its attachments, separately send a copy of the order to the arresting agency, the prosecutor and the clerk under § 46-18-1110(2)(b), allow thirty days for the confirmation letter, then re-verify on both portals and by re-pulling the CRISS record. The instructions carry the once-in-a-lifetime warning at the top and say nothing about whether the participant may later deny the conviction.

rules.filing: Unit 1 is a civil petition filed on paper with the clerk of a district court in a judicial district where at least one conviction occurred (§ 46-18-1105). Local district court filing rules apply and the Office of the Court Administrator Court Locator is the published route to local rules and contact information; confirm with the clerk before filing. Unit 2 is a mailed submission to DOJ CRISS after the order issues. Whether any district permits or requires self-represented e-filing for this petition type is unresolved.
rules.fees: $120 for civil commencement of an action by a petitioner, per the Montana Clerks of District Courts civil fee schedule updated May 2024 and issued under §§ 25-1-201, 25-1-202, 3-1-317, 50-15-301 and 25-9-506. The base statutory figure in § 25-1-201(1)(a) is $90; use the published schedule total for the participant-facing number. No fee is charged for the CRISS request. The participant pays for the background check, court document copies and the fingerprinting.
rules.feeWaiver: By statement of inability to pay court costs and fees. The judiciary and Montana Legal Services Association route participants to the MLSA interactive Statement of Inability to Pay Court Costs and Fees plus a proposed order. That form carries the same non-commercial-use restriction as ER-100 and ER-200, so LegalEase links the participant to the published form and does not reproduce it. Whether a court-approved statewide fee-waiver form exists is unresolved.
rules.notice: § 46-18-1106(1) requires notice to every prosecution office that prosecuted an offence for which expungement is requested. § 46-18-1106(2) gives that office fourteen days from receiving the petition to attempt to notify any victim and to document the attempt. There is no statutory deadline for the prosecution office to respond to the petition itself. § 46-18-1107(1) additionally places on the prosecution office the duty to verify that the petitioner is not detained, charged or subject to pending charges.
rules.service: Mail, hand delivery or email of a file-stamped copy of the petition to each prosecuting office, after filing. Montana files first and then serves; do not reverse it. Victims are notified by the prosecution office, not by the participant.
rules.participantSignature: The petitioner signs the petition under a declaration under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of Montana, giving the city and state where signed, and separately signs the CRISS form. LegalEase leaves both blank.
rules.notarization: none. A declaration under penalty of perjury is used instead.

legalDesignDecision.rationale: The review approved this track with limitations and the composed structure follows the statute rather than the workflow. The two units are genuinely distinct legal acts: a district-court petition under Part 11, and a separate participant-initiated submission to the Department of Justice that § 46-18-1110(2)(b) places on the participant by name, with a different destination and a different form. Record gathering, fingerprinting, filing, service and verification are instructions inside those units, not units of their own. The court stage is custom_pleading for two independent reasons: Part 11 prescribes no form and no statewide form has been adopted under the § 46-18-1111 rulemaking authority, and the only published petition and order, ER-100 and ER-200, are licensed for non-commercial use only and cannot lawfully be shipped in a paid packet. The DOJ stage is official_pdf_fill because the CRISS form is a genuine agency form with no use restriction and is what the statute means by a form prepared by the department of justice. The once-in-a-lifetime rule is enforced by a hard confirmation gate before generation, the FD-258 dependency is sequenced at the front of the task list, and the § 46-18-1108(2) rehabilitation and public-safety argument is a self-help boundary that LegalEase never authors.

limitations.statement: Montana's three words are not interchangeable and participant copy must keep them apart. Expungement under § 46-18-1103(1) means to permanently destroy, delete or erase a record from the criminal history record information system maintained by the Department of Justice. What happens at the courts, law-enforcement agencies and prosecutors' offices is sealing, not destruction (§ 46-18-1110(2)(a)). Removal is the DOJ term for deleting a non-conviction record. Redesignation and resentencing are MMRTA outcomes and are neither.

provenance.sourceStatement: Correct jurisdiction-specific terminology: "Expungement." Montana defines the word narrowly at § 46-18-1103(1): to permanently destroy, delete, or erase a record of an offense from the criminal history record information system maintained by the Department of Justice. What happens at the courts, law enforcement agencies, and prosecutors' offices is sealing, not destruction (§ 46-18-1110(2)(a)). Do not use the two words interchangeably in participant copy.

limitations.statement: Montana has no general felony expungement and no automatic conviction sealing. Part 11 reaches misdemeanours only. The only felony relief is marijuana-specific under § 16-12-113 and trafficking-survivor vacatur under § 46-18-608. There is no Clean Slate analogue, and eligibility copy must say this plainly rather than implying a felony pathway exists.

tracks.legalName: Petition for Expungement or Redesignation of a Marijuana Conviction, Sentence Completed (Mont. Code Ann. § 16-12-113(5)-(10), (12))

controllingAuthority.summary: Under § 16-12-113(5)(a) a person who has COMPLETED a sentence for an act that is now permitted under Title 16, chapter 12, or that is now punishable by a lesser sentence under that chapter than the person was awarded, may petition for expungement of the conviction or for redesignation of the conviction as a misdemeanour or as a civil infraction. Section 16-12-113(5)(b) requires service on the county attorney for the county in which the petition is filed — the statute keys service to the county of FILING, not the county of prosecution. Section 16-12-113(6) directs the court to presume the petitioner satisfies the criteria unless the county attorney provides the court with a reasonable basis on which the petitioner does not; the 2021 amendment lowered that prosecutorial burden from clear and convincing evidence to providing a reasonable basis. Once the criteria are satisfied the court shall redesignate or expunge. Section 16-12-113(7) provides that unless requested by the applicant, no hearing is necessary. Section 16-12-113(8) provides that a felony conviction designated as a misdemeanour or civil infraction must be considered a misdemeanour or civil infraction for all purposes, and a misdemeanour designated as a civil infraction must be considered a civil infraction for all purposes. Section 16-12-113(9) waives no other right or remedy, § 16-12-113(10) preserves the finality of judgments in cases outside the chapter, § 16-12-113(11) applies the relief equally to juvenile cases, and § 16-12-113(12) expressly preserves the right to petition separately for misdemeanour expungement under Title 46, chapter 18, part 11. Procedure is governed by the Temporary Rules adopted by Montana Supreme Court order AF 22-0129, filed 15 March 2022, and the Office of the Court Administrator publishes Form B with a Certificate of Service and a Proposed Order. Enacted as Sec. 36, I.M. No. 190, effective 1 January 2021, amended by Sec. 48, Ch. 576, L. 2021.

exclusions: Acts that remain criminal at the same level under Title 16, chapter 12. The whole test is whether the conduct is now permitted or is now punishable by a lesser sentence.
Non-marijuana controlled substance convictions.
Convictions from out-of-state, federal or Tribal courts.
A participant who is still serving the sentence, who belongs on the currently-serving track under § 16-12-113(1) rather than this one.
Anything outside Title 16, chapter 12: § 16-12-113(10) preserves the finality of judgments in those cases.

units.label: MMRTA Form B petition in the sentencing court, with certificate of service and proposed order
units.description: The court stage. One complete set per conviction — MMRTA Form B, the OCA Certificate of Service and the OCA Proposed Order — filed in the court that sentenced the participant, with a copy of the participant's Montana Department of Justice criminal record attached, which Form B marks required. The Office of the Court Administrator publishes the whole set under Montana Supreme Court authority in AF 22-0129, the forms carry no use restriction, and they encode the statutory offence list, the required attachments, the § 16-12-113(7) hearing election and the § 16-12-113(5)(b) service requirement. LegalEase completes the caption for the correct court level, the participant's identity and case facts, the offence selection the participant makes from the enumerated list, and the conviction date. It does not complete the narrative explaining why the conviction is eligible, and it does not choose among expungement, misdemeanour redesignation and civil-infraction redesignation. The Certificate of Service names the county attorney for the county in which the petition is filed. The Proposed Order leaves every judicial finding and the signature blank.

units.label: DOJ CRISS submission after an expungement order
units.description: The Department of Justice stage, and a separate legal unit with its own destination and its own participant submission: the court order does not itself clear the DOJ criminal history record. LegalEase completes the participant-owned fields of the CRISS Expungement/Removal Request Form and supplies the mailing checklist and verification steps; the participant encloses the original or certified court judgment and the court order of expungement and mails them to CRISS. This unit applies where the outcome is EXPUNGEMENT. Where the participant instead obtains redesignation as a misdemeanour or as a civil infraction, the conviction is not expunged and there is no DOJ deletion stage to complete, so the unit does not apply and the packet says so rather than sending a request that will be refused. No FD-258 fingerprint card is required for the marijuana request type, unlike the misdemeanour expungement track.

geography.venue: Whichever court sentenced the participant. Form B provides three caption options — Montana Judicial District Court by county, Justice Court of a county, and Municipal or City Court — and recites that venue is proper because it is the court in which the participant was sentenced. This is a materially different venue rule from the misdemeanour expungement track, which always goes to District Court.

destination.name: The sentencing court, then the Department of Justice
destination.detail: Unit 1 is filed in the sentencing court under that court's rules, including local filing rules. Unit 2 is mailed to Montana Department of Justice, Division of Criminal Investigation, CRISS Expungement, 2225 11th Ave., P.O. Box 201403, Helena, MT 59620. Phone (406) 444-3625. Email dojcriss@mt.gov.

components.notes: MMRTA Form B, Petition for Expungement or Redesignation of Conviction, published by the Office of the Court Administrator under AF 22-0129 and retained by Master Library Edition 1.1 as a source-gated asset. One per conviction. It enumerates criminal distribution of dangerous drugs (marijuana) under § 45-9-101; criminal possession of dangerous drugs (marijuana) under § 45-9-102; criminal possession with intent to distribute (marijuana) under § 45-9-103; criminal production or manufacture of dangerous drugs (marijuana) under § 45-9-110; criminal possession of drug paraphernalia (marijuana) under § 45-10-103; and manufacture or delivery of drug paraphernalia (marijuana) under § 45-10-104, plus a free-text specify-offence line. The participant elects the outcome sought and, where a hearing is wanted, elects that too.

The OCA Certificate of Service for an MMRTA petition, retained by Edition 1.1 as a source-gated asset. Form B marks it required and § 16-12-113(5)(b) requires service on the county attorney for the county in which the petition is filed. Note the statute keys service to the county of FILING, not the county of prosecution.

The OCA Proposed Order Granting Expungement, Resentencing, or Redesignation Under MMRTA, retained by Edition 1.1 as a source-gated asset. The OCA instructions recommend it and publish the template. Judge findings and signature are left blank; Edition 1.1 records the same requirement in the asset's own note.

Attachment checklist for unit 1: a copy of the participant's criminal record from the Montana Department of Justice, which Form B marks required; and, recommended by OCA, a copy of the judgment or sentencing order for the conviction. LegalEase names them and the participant obtains and attaches them; neither is inspected or authenticated.

components.conditionDescription: Unit 2. Generated only where the court grants EXPUNGEMENT; a redesignation outcome has no DOJ deletion stage.
components.notes: The CRISS Expungement/Removal Request Form for the post-order stage, with the original or certified court judgment and the court order of expungement enclosed. No FD-258 card is required for this request type.

Sequenced instructions across both units: obtain the DOJ criminal record, which is a required attachment; identify the sentencing court using the OCA Court Locator and confirm that court's local filing rules, which the OCA instructions expressly require; prepare one complete form set per conviction; sign, because the OCA instructions state the court will not consider an unsigned petition; file and pay the fee for that court level, or seek a waiver; serve the county attorney for the county of filing; allow the twenty-one-day county attorney response window; the court rules with or without a hearing depending on the participant's election; then, if expungement was granted, complete the CRISS submission; then verify on both Montana Public Access Portals and by re-pulling the CRISS record. The instructions state plainly that a redesignation outcome does not produce a DOJ deletion, and that the court order alone does not clear the DOJ record.

What is your date of birth?

Which offence were you convicted of? Choose from the list: criminal distribution of dangerous drugs (marijuana); criminal possession of dangerous drugs (marijuana); criminal possession with intent to distribute (marijuana); criminal production or manufacture of dangerous drugs (marijuana); criminal possession of drug paraphernalia (marijuana); manufacture or delivery of drug paraphernalia (marijuana); or another offence you will name.

In your own words, why is this conviction eligible — what makes the conduct something that is now allowed under Montana's marijuana law, or something that would now carry a lesser sentence?

rules.filing: File one complete set per conviction in the court that sentenced the participant, under that court's rules including local filing rules. The OCA instructions expressly require the participant to follow all applicable filing rules and route them to the Court Locator. The court will not consider an unsigned petition. Unit 2 is a separate mailed submission to DOJ CRISS after an expungement order.
rules.fees: The participant is responsible for filing fees and other costs. In District Court the civil commencement fee is $120 per the Montana Clerks of District Courts civil fee schedule updated May 2024. Justice, Municipal and City Court fees are different and were not resolved, so the packet branches on court level and tells the participant to confirm with the clerk. No fee is charged for the CRISS request.
rules.feeWaiver: The OCA instructions route participants to the Statement of Inability to Pay Court Costs and Fees on montanalawhelp.org. That form carries a non-commercial-use restriction, so LegalEase links to it and does not reproduce it.
rules.notice: Service on the county attorney for the county in which the petition is filed (§ 16-12-113(5)(b)), evidenced by the OCA Certificate of Service filed alongside the petition. The county attorney has twenty-one days to respond in opposition per the OCA instructions, and must provide the court with a reasonable basis on which the petitioner does not satisfy the criteria (§ 16-12-113(6)). No hearing is necessary unless the applicant requests one (§ 16-12-113(7)).
rules.service: As stated on the OCA Certificate of Service, with or before filing. Note that the statute keys service to the county of filing rather than the county of prosecution.
rules.participantSignature: The participant signs Form B and separately signs the CRISS form. LegalEase leaves both blank.

legalDesignDecision.rationale: The review approved this track with limitations and the composed structure follows the law. Unit 1 is official_pdf_fill because the Office of the Court Administrator publishes a complete, purpose-built form set under Montana Supreme Court authority in AF 22-0129 — Form B, a Certificate of Service and a Proposed Order — which carries no use restriction and encodes the statutory offence list, the required attachments, the hearing election and the service requirement. Drafting a custom pleading would discard all of that and depart from what Montana county attorneys and clerks already see. Unit 2 is a genuinely separate legal act with a different destination and a different form, and it is conditional: it applies where the outcome is expungement and does not apply where the participant instead obtains redesignation, because there is then no DOJ deletion to request. The two forms formerly recorded as missing from the archive, the OCA Certificate of Service and the OCA Proposed Order, are retained by Master Library Edition 1.1 and that limitation is closed. What LegalEase never does is choose among the three statutory outcomes or author the eligibility narrative.

limitations.statement: Montana's three words are not interchangeable and participant copy must keep them apart. Expungement under § 46-18-1103(1) means to permanently destroy, delete or erase a record from the criminal history record information system maintained by the Department of Justice. What happens at the courts, law-enforcement agencies and prosecutors' offices is sealing, not destruction (§ 46-18-1110(2)(a)). Removal is the DOJ term for deleting a non-conviction record. Redesignation and resentencing are MMRTA outcomes and are neither.

provenance.sourceStatement: Correct jurisdiction-specific terminology: "Expungement." What happens at the courts, law enforcement agencies, and prosecutors' offices is sealing, not destruction (§ 46-18-1110(2)(a)). Do not use the two words interchangeably in participant copy.

controllingAuthority.summary: Under § 16-12-113(1) a person CURRENTLY SERVING a sentence for an act that is permitted under Title 16, chapter 12, or that is punishable by a lesser sentence under that chapter than the person was awarded, may petition for expungement or resentencing. Section 16-12-113(2) directs the court to presume the petitioner satisfies the criteria unless the county attorney provides a reasonable basis otherwise, and, where the criteria are satisfied, to grant the petition UNLESS the court determines that granting it would pose an unreasonable risk of danger to public safety. That public-safety override does not appear in the subsection (6) pathway used by the completed-sentence track, and it is the principal reason the two are separate mechanisms rather than branches. Section 16-12-113(3) requires credit for time already served and prohibits supervision after resentencing; § 16-12-113(4) prohibits a term longer than the original sentence and prohibits reinstatement of charges dismissed under a negotiated plea agreement. Sections 16-12-114 through 16-12-116 define an expungement or resentencing of marijuana conviction court and authorise appointment of a decriminalized marijuana conviction expungement judge with the authority and power of an elected district court judge. Procedure is governed by the AF 22-0129 Temporary Rules and the Office of the Court Administrator publishes Form A specifically for the currently-serving posture, with the same Certificate of Service and Proposed Order.

exclusions: Acts that remain criminal at the same level under Title 16, chapter 12.
Non-marijuana controlled substance convictions.
Convictions from out-of-state, federal or Tribal courts.
A participant who has completed the sentence, who belongs on the completed-sentence track under § 16-12-113(5).
Relief may still be refused where the court determines that granting the petition would pose an unreasonable risk of danger to public safety (§ 16-12-113(2)). That override is unique to this track.

units.label: MMRTA Form A petition in the sentencing court, with certificate of service and proposed order
units.description: The court stage, and the substantive heart of the track. MMRTA Form A is published by the Office of the Court Administrator specifically for the currently-serving posture: the caption, the 'I am currently serving my sentence for this conviction' recital and the resentencing election are all built into it. The adopted Batch 2 resolution memorandum controls here and is explicit that Form A is a packet product and that the currently-serving posture is a scope restriction and a substantive-choice warning rather than a reason to downgrade the mechanism to guidance. LegalEase completes the caption for the correct court level, the participant's identity and case facts, the offence selection the participant makes from the enumerated list, and the conviction date, and assembles the OCA Certificate of Service and the OCA Proposed Order. It does not choose between expungement and resentencing, does not calculate a resentencing result, and does not author any public-safety argument. Required attachments are the participant's DOJ criminal record and the supporting court documents.

Where the court grants EXPUNGEMENT the participant must separately submit the CRISS Expungement/Removal Request Form with the court judgment and the expungement order, because the court order does not itself clear the DOJ criminal history record. Where the outcome is RESENTENCING rather than expungement the conviction stands with a modified sentence, there is nothing for DOJ to delete, and this unit does not apply — the packet says so plainly rather than sending a request that will be refused. That conditionality is why the unit exists as a distinct unit rather than as a step inside unit 1.

controllingAuthority.summary: Section 46-18-204 has two limbs sharing one process, one destination, one document set and one legal effect, differing only on whether relief is mandatory. Under § 46-18-204(1)(a), on a FELONY deferred imposition, after termination of the deferral period or upon termination of the time remaining under § 46-18-208, the court SHALL strike the plea of guilty or nolo contendere or the verdict of guilty and order the charge dismissed, PROVIDED THAT a petition for revocation under § 46-18-203 has not been filed. Under § 46-18-204(1)(b), on a MISDEMEANOUR deferred imposition, upon motion of the court, the defendant or the defendant's attorney, the court MAY allow withdrawal of the plea or strike the verdict and order dismissal — discretionary, with no statutory factors. After dismissal, all records and data relating to the charge are confidential criminal justice information as defined in § 44-5-103, and public access may be obtained only by district court order upon good cause shown. This is sealing, not expungement: the record is not destroyed, and per DOJ the agencies listed in § 44-5-103 retain access to the sealed record in its entirety, DOJ specifically naming law enforcement including the military and Border Patrol. Section 46-18-204(2) puts the second stage on the participant: a copy of the order of dismissal must be sent to the prosecutor and to the Department of Justice with the DOJ form. Amended by Sec. 25, Ch. 321, L. 2017; no amendment since.

exclusions: A felony case in which a petition for revocation under § 46-18-203 was filed. That is the operative bar on the mandatory limb and it defeats § 46-18-204(1)(a) outright.

A SUSPENDED sentence. The published guidance states expressly that it does not apply to suspended sentences, and a participant who received a suspended rather than a deferred sentence is outside this route entirely.
A participant seeking early termination under § 46-18-208 rather than post-completion dismissal.
A deferral period that has not terminated and where no early termination under § 46-18-208 has occurred.
A case the court has already dismissed and sealed on its own, which the published guidance warns may have happened. The clerk-contact step is designed to catch this before anything is filed.

units.label: Motion in the sentencing court to strike the plea or verdict, dismiss the charge and seal the case
units.description: The court stage. A motion to strike the plea or verdict, dismiss the charge and seal the case, with a certificate of service and a proposed order, filed in the court that issued the deferred sentence, under the SAME case number as the original criminal case. This is a motion in the existing criminal case rather than a new civil action, which is why no new filing fee is ordinarily expected. Section 46-18-204 prescribes no form, and the only published forms — DS-100 and DS-200 — carry the same non-commercial-use restriction as the misdemeanour expungement packet and cannot be shipped in a paid packet, so LegalEase drafts its own. The motion pleads the crime of conviction and whether it is a misdemeanour or a felony; whether the defendant pleaded guilty or nolo contendere or was found guilty by verdict; the date of sentencing and the fact of a deferred sentence; that the period of deferral has expired; that the defendant complied with all conditions; and that the prosecuting agency did not file a petition to revoke during the deferral period. The felony limb recites the mandatory shall and the no-revocation-petition proviso expressly; the misdemeanour limb is pleaded as discretionary. The prayer asks the court to strike the plea or verdict, dismiss the charge, seal the case, classify all records and data as confidential criminal justice information accessible to the public only by district court order upon good cause shown, and send a copy of the order to the prosecuting agency, and recites that the defendant will be responsible for providing a copy to the Department of Justice. localFormOverride is set because the published guidance acknowledges that individual courts may have their own procedures or different forms, and a court's current local form takes precedence over the drafted motion.

Without this stage the DOJ criminal history record continues to show the charge.

tracks.legalName: Non-Conviction Record Removal Request to DOJ CRISS (Mont. Code Ann. § 44-5-202(8))

controllingAuthority.summary: Montana distinguishes removal, where the record is deleted from the database and hard copy destroyed, from sealing under § 46-18-204, where the record persists but is confidential. Section 44-5-202(8), read with § 44-5-213(2), compels the disposition to be reported to the state repository within fourteen business days, requires photographs and fingerprints to be returned to the originating agency which shall expunge all copies, and provides that a criminal justice agency may not maintain any copies. DOJ publishes a single agency form, the Expungement/Removal Request Form, with a dedicated Non-Conviction Removal request type, and its published list of eligible dispositions is charges dismissed, deferred prosecution dismissed, acquitted, charges dropped and charges not filed; in statute the categories are released without the filing of charges, charges that did not result in a conviction, and a conviction later invalidated. Two gaps must be recorded rather than papered over. First, § 44-5-202 is titled Photographs and fingerprints and subsection (8) by its terms compels expungement of PHOTOGRAPHS AND FINGERPRINTS; it does not on its face compel deletion of the criminal history record entry itself, and § 44-5-212 separately limits expunging, purging or destroying criminal justice information. DOJ nonetheless treats § 44-5-202(8) as the authority for removing non-conviction arrest data and instructs participants to quote it, so LegalEase follows the published practice but does not represent the outcome as legally guaranteed beyond the photographs and fingerprints. Second, § 44-5-202(8) reaches the state repository and originating agencies and does NOT reach court records; Montana has no comparable authority to seal non-conviction court records and no centralised court records system, so a participant who succeeds here may still find the case on a county court portal.

Court records. § 44-5-202(8) reaches the state repository and originating agencies only, and the case may remain publicly searchable on a county court portal.

components.notes: The CRISS Expungement/Removal Request Form with the Non-Conviction Removal box checked, updated 29 April 2024 and retained by Master Library Edition 1.1 as the Montana supporting-process asset. The fields are almost entirely factual, which makes it a clean fill: full legal name, date of arrest or fingerprinting, the charges, date of birth, the optional last four digits of the Social Security number, return address, phone and email. LegalEase completes the participant-owned fields and leaves the signature and date for the participant. It is the required vehicle, carries no use restriction, and there is no court filing so no pleading is possible.

Attachment checklist. The 2024 form lists the court judgment for this request type. The 2023 version additionally required a legible photocopy of valid photo identification — a state-issued ID, driver's licence or passport — for the Non-Conviction Removal type, and because the two versions disagree the packet includes photo identification BY DEFAULT, which is the fail-closed reading. Where the DOJ record is incomplete, CRISS will attempt to obtain court documentation of the outcome and, failing that, the participant must supply it.

Instructions covering: run a Montana public criminal history record check through CHOPRS or by mail FIRST, which DOJ instructs participants to do before submitting, allowing for a hold of up to seventy-two hours; search both Montana Public Access Portals; classify the disposition against DOJ's published list; complete and mail the form with the judgment and photo identification; allow thirty days for processing, after which CRISS issues a letter explaining the outcome; then re-verify by re-pulling the CRISS record. The instructions state in terms that this route does not reach court records and that the case may still appear on a county court portal, and that the outcome is not legally guaranteed beyond the photographs and fingerprints.

tracks.legalName: Automatic Non-Conviction Removal for Post-July-2017 Dispositions (Mont. Code Ann. § 44-5-202(8))

controllingAuthority.summary: Section 44-5-202(8), as amended by Ch. 321, L. 2017 effective 1 July 2017 and read with § 44-5-213(2), underpins a DOJ practice of removing non-conviction arrest data without any participant request. The Montana Department of Justice states on its Non-Conviction Removal and Sealing page that after 1 July 2017 CRISS will automatically remove all non-conviction arrest data per § 44-5-202 and that NO Record Removal Form is required. The trigger is the court's report of the disposition to the state repository, which the statute requires within fourteen business days. Relief is mandatory and automatic, there is no waiting period and no case-count limit, and there is no petition, application, motion or form for a participant to submit. The only practical question on this route is whether a record that has not been removed is ineligible or is simply the product of a court that failed to report the disposition, which is a records problem rather than a legal one.

exclusions: Dispositions occurring before 1 July 2017, which are not reached by the automatic practice and go to the non-conviction removal request route instead.

legalDesignDecision.rationale: Process guidance is retained here on the narrow and substantive ground that DOJ states expressly that no Record Removal Form is required and that there is no participant filing for the automatic mechanism — not because an agency controls the result and not because a form is missing. Relief occurs automatically once the court reports the disposition, so there is nothing for LegalEase to generate. What LegalEase does provide is the verification layer: the CHOPRS check, both Montana Public Access Portal searches, the court-reporting correction script, and the fallback routing to the non-conviction removal request route where the automatic removal did not occur. That fallback request belongs to the separate removal track and is not treated as evidence that this mechanism has a filing of its own. No form is generated for this route.

limitations.statement: Montana's three words are not interchangeable and participant copy must keep them apart. Expungement under § 46-18-1103(1) means to permanently destroy, delete or erase a record from the criminal history record information system maintained by the Department of Justice. What happens at the courts, law-enforcement agencies and prosecutors' offices is sealing, not destruction (§ 46-18-1110(2)(a)). Removal is the DOJ term for deleting a non-conviction record. Redesignation and resentencing are MMRTA outcomes and are neither.

provenance.sourceStatement: Correct jurisdiction-specific terminology: "Expungement." Montana defines the word narrowly at § 46-18-1103(1): to permanently destroy, delete, or erase a record of an offense from the criminal history record information system maintained by the Department of Justice. What happens at the courts, law enforcement agencies, and prosecutors' offices is sealing, not destruction (§ 46-18-1110(2)(a)). Do not use the two words interchangeably in participant copy.

limitations.statement: A DOJ removal or expungement does not reach public county court records. Montana has no centralised court records system, so each county court must be searched separately, and a participant who successfully clears the DOJ record may still find the case on a county court portal. Participant-facing copy must say so.

provenance.sourceStatement: A second gap with real participant impact. § 44-5-202(8) reaches the state repository and originating agencies. It does not reach court records. Montana has no comparable authority to seal non-conviction court records, and the state has no centralized court records system, so each county court must be searched separately.
